title: Resources and workflows
text:
The resource request affects both whether a job succeeds and how easily Slurm can find space for it:

--time sets the maximum running time.
--mem reserves memory for the job.
--cpus-per-task assigns CPUs to one task.

Too little time or memory can cause a job to be stopped before it finishes. Requesting far more than the job uses can make it wait longer and leaves resources unavailable to other users. Additional CPUs help only when the program is designed to use them.
Start with a reasonable estimate and a modest margin. After the job finishes, compare the request with its actual use:
seff <job-id>
sacct -j <job-id> --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS
seff provides an approachable summary of CPU and memory efficiency. MaxRSS reports peak resident memory and may use suffixes such as K, M, or G. Use these results to refine the next request.

title: Resources and workflows
text:
Interactive jobs
An interactive job provides a shell on a compute node. It is useful for testing commands, debugging, installing packages, or doing short exploratory work before submitting a batch job.
srun --time=01:00:00 --partition=interact \
  --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4g \
  --pty /bin/bash
Slurm waits for the requested resources and then changes the prompt to a compute node. Run exit when finished to release the allocation and return to the login node. Long or repeatable analyses should be submitted as batch jobs so they can continue after you disconnect.

title: Resources and workflows
text:
Job arrays
A job array applies the same workflow to many files or parameter settings. One submission script is run multiple times, and each task receives a different number in $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:
#SBATCH --array=1-12
Arrays are useful for high-throughput work because their tasks can run independently on whatever nodes are available. Test one task before submitting hundreds, and use a concurrency limit such as --array=1-500%50 when appropriate. Module 4 includes a complete R job-array example.

title: Resources and workflows
text:
Partitions
A partition is a logical group or queue of computing resources with a particular purpose or set of limits. Longleaf includes resources for standard CPU jobs, interactive work, data movement, and GPU jobs.
Most ordinary jobs can use the default placement rather than naming a partition. Interactive sessions use the interact partition, while specialized jobs may need a partition that provides the required hardware. Available resources and limits can change, so consult UNC Research Computing’s current Longleaf documentation for unusual runtime, memory, or GPU requirements.






WarningKeep heavy work off login nodes



Login nodes are shared entry points. Use them to organize files, edit scripts, and submit jobs. Resource-intensive analyses should run through Slurm on compute nodes.

title: Resources and workflows
text:
Summary

Prepare files and submit jobs from a login node.
Slurm sends computational work to compute nodes.
Use squeue for active jobs and sacct or seff after completion.
Request time, memory, and CPUs based on what the job actually needs.
Load required software explicitly inside job scripts.

title: Working on Longleaf
text:
Software modules
Basic Linux tools are available when you log in. Longleaf uses software modules to provide additional programs and to let different versions of the same program coexist.



Task
Command




See available software
module avail


Search for R modules
module avail r


Load the default R module
module add r


Load a particular version
module add r/<version>


Show loaded modules
module list


Unload all modules
module purge



For example, module add r makes the default R installation available in the current session. Use module avail r first if a project requires a particular version.

Put module commands in job scripts
By default, sbatch carries much of the environment from the submitting shell into a job. A reproducible script should not depend on whatever happened to be loaded at submission time. UNC recommends explicitly resetting the modules and then loading what the job needs:
module purge
module add r
module save can arrange for a preferred set of modules to load at future logins, but batch jobs should still contain their own module purge and module add commands.


Pin versions when reproducibility requires it
The default version of a program can change. A short exploratory task may be fine with module add r; a project that must be rerun months later should record and load the version it used. Replace <version> with one shown by module avail r:
module purge
module add r/<version>

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf is UNC-Chapel Hill’s shared research computing cluster. It gives researchers access to computing power, memory, storage, and specialized software beyond what is typically available on a personal computer.
Rather than relying on a single machine, Longleaf brings together many computers and makes their resources available to researchers across the university.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf is UNC-Chapel Hill’s shared research computing cluster. It gives researchers access to computing power, memory, storage, and specialized software beyond what is typically available on a personal computer.
Rather than relying on a single machine, Longleaf brings together many computers and makes their resources available to researchers across the university.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Why use a computing cluster?
A computing cluster can provide:

more processors and memory than a personal computer
capacity for computations that are too large or numerous for a laptop
access to research software and specialized hardware
large working storage for research data
scheduling and job management for a shared system

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
High-performance and high-throughput computing
Two terms are commonly used to describe work performed on computing clusters:







High-performance computing (HPC)
High-throughput computing (HTC)




Focuses on completing one large computation quickly
Focuses on completing many computations over time


Often divides one calculation among processors or nodes working together
Often consists of independent serial or single-node jobs


Example: one large simulation
Example: applying the same analysis to many files or parameter combinations



HPC and HTC describe patterns of computing rather than entirely separate kinds of machines. A shared computing cluster may support both patterns.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf’s focus
Longleaf was designed with high-throughput and data-intensive research in mind. This includes work involving:

large numbers of serial or single-node jobs
substantial memory requirements
large datasets
frequent reading and writing of data

This design makes Longleaf useful for research in which the main challenge is the number, size, or resource requirements of the computations.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Computing resources
Longleaf includes different kinds of compute nodes for different kinds of work:

General-purpose nodes support many common research applications.
High-I/O nodes support work that reads or writes large amounts of data.
Large-memory nodes support analyses that must hold substantial amounts of data in memory.
GPU nodes support software that can use graphics processors for computation.

The available resources continue to change as the cluster evolves, so current hardware specifications should be checked in UNC Research Computing documentation when they matter for a project.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
When might Longleaf help?
Examples relevant to psychology, statistics, and related fields include:

applying the same analysis to many participants, datasets, or files
fitting many model specifications
running bootstrap, permutation, or simulation studies
processing files that are too large for a personal computer
running an analysis that requires more memory than a laptop provides
using research software or GPU resources that are unavailable locally

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Where this workshop ends up
Module 4 is the payoff, and it follows the high-throughput pattern above with R:

Interactive R, for testing and debugging (Example 1).
One R script as one job, submitted, monitored, and read back (Example 2).
A simulation with twelve conditions as twelve jobs, submitted with one command and collected into one data frame (Example 3).

Modules 2 and 3 exist to make those three steps routine: getting onto the cluster and moving files, then describing, submitting, and reading jobs.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
A shared resource
Many researchers use Longleaf at the same time. Users describe the work they want to run and the resources it needs. A scheduler then determines when and where that work will run.
The next page follows that process from a user’s computer to a Longleaf compute node.

title: R on Longleaf
text: Guiding question: When should R be run interactively, and when should it become a scheduled job?

title: R on Longleaf
text:
R installations on Longleaf
R is installed as a software module (Module 3), with several versions available. Nothing is loaded when you log in, so every session, and every job script, starts by loading one:
module avail r        # list the R modules; the default is marked (D)
module add r          # load the default version
module add r/<version> # or pin a version shown by module avail r
R --version           # confirm which R you have

title: R on Longleaf
text:
Where packages live
R looks for packages in a short list of folders. On Longleaf, two of them matter:

The R module’s library. The packages that ship with R, and any that Research Computing has installed centrally, live inside the R installation that module add r loads. Everyone can use them, and nobody can change them.
Your personal library. Anything you install yourself goes into a folder in your home directory. R creates it for you the first time you install a package. The default location is ~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.4, where 4.4 matches the version of R you loaded.

Inside R, .libPaths() prints these folders in the order R searches them.
Two consequences follow from that layout. Your home directory is shared storage, so a package installed once is available in RStudio Server, interactive sessions, and batch jobs alike, as long as they load the same R module. And the personal library belongs to one R version: patch releases such as 4.4.0 and 4.4.2 share it, but an R module with a different minor version looks in a different folder, so packages installed under the old version are not found until you install them again.

title: R on Longleaf
section: Interactive R or a scheduled job?
text:
Interactive R or a scheduled job?







Use interactive R when…
Use a scheduled job when…




testing a short command
the analysis may run for a long time


checking that packages load
the work should continue after disconnecting


debugging a small example
the analysis needs substantial memory or CPUs


exploring an unfamiliar dataset
the same analysis will be repeated

title: R on Longleaf
text:
Installing packages
Install packages from an interactive R session, not from a job script. Example 1 below walks through it: load R, call install.packages(), answer yes when R offers to create a personal library, and confirm with library(). Anything installed that way lands in your personal library, where every later session and job that loads the same R module can find it.
Packages with compiled code take a few minutes to build. That is normal; wait for the prompt to return.






TipInstall once, interactively



A job script should load R and run your code, nothing more. Installing inside a job is slow, and the twelve tasks of a job array all trying to install the same package at once will interfere with each other. Install in an interactive session, confirm library() works, then submit.



Installing from a file you upload
Some packages are not on CRAN: one a collaborator sent you, one you are developing, or one you downloaded from GitHub as a source archive. In that case, upload the package’s .tar.gz file to your home directory on Longleaf with FileZilla, then point install.packages() at the file instead of a repository:
install.packages("~/mypackage_0.1.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
repos = NULL tells R to install from the file. R does not download dependencies in this mode, so if the installation stops with there is no package called 'xyz', install xyz from CRAN first and run the command again. The package lands in the same personal library as everything else.
If you have the package as a folder rather than an archive, build the archive on your laptop first. From the folder’s parent directory, R CMD build mypackage produces the .tar.gz file to upload.

title: R on Longleaf
text:
Three examples
The rest of this module follows the progression most projects take:

Interactive R, for testing, debugging, and installing packages.
A single scheduled job that runs one R script once.
A batch of scheduled jobs that run the same script under many parameter settings.

The files for Examples 2 and 3 are in the examples/ folder of this site’s repository, and each file is linked below. To get all of them at once, download examples.zip and unzip it on your computer. It unpacks to one examples folder with a subfolder per example, ready to drag to Longleaf with FileZilla. In the commands that follow, replace <onyen> with your ONYEN.

title: R on Longleaf
text:
Example 1 · Interactive R
The quickest way to use R on Longleaf is to load it and start it, right where you land after logging in:
ssh <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu
module add r
R
Inside R, confirm which R you have and try a few commands:
R.version.string
Sys.info()[["nodename"]]   # the login node you are on
x <- rnorm(1e6); mean(x)

Installing a package
Stay in the same R session. This is where every package you need on Longleaf gets installed, so install one now:
install.packages("lavaan", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
The repos argument skips the CRAN mirror menu that R otherwise shows in a terminal. The first time you install anything, R notices that it cannot write to the module’s library and asks two questions. Answer yes to both:
Would you like to use a personal library instead? (yes/No/cancel) yes
Would you like to create a personal library
'~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.4'
to install packages into? (yes/No/cancel) yes
R downloads the package and the packages it depends on, builds them, and prints * DONE (lavaan) when it is finished. From then on, every install.packages() call goes straight to your personal library without asking. Confirm the package loads and see where it went:
library(lavaan)
find.package("lavaan")   # the folder it was installed into
The path printed is inside your home directory, so the package is now available to RStudio Server and to the batch jobs in Examples 2 and 3, as long as they load the same R module. Leave R with q(), and answer n when it offers to save the workspace.


From the browser
Open OnDemand, the web portal introduced in Module 2 at https://ondemand.rc.unc.edu, has an RStudio Server app under Interactive Apps. Choose the number of hours, CPUs, memory, and the R module, and RStudio opens on a compute node in a browser tab. UNC recommends requesting at least two CPUs for RStudio sessions.

title: R on Longleaf
section: Example 2 · Submitting a single R job
text:
Example 2 · Submitting a single R job
The simplest scheduled workflow: one R script that runs once and saves its output. The files are in examples/example2_single_job/.



File
Purpose




hello_longleaf.R
The R script. Simulates data, fits lm(), and saves a list to results/hello_results.rds.


submit_single.sl
The Slurm submission script: the resources the job needs and the command it runs.


logs/
Where Slurm writes the job’s console output (.out) and errors (.err).


results/
Where the R script writes its .rds file.




The submission script


submit_single.sl

#!/bin/bash
# submit_single.sl -- SLURM submission script for Example 2 (one R job)
#
# Submit from inside this folder with:   sbatch submit_single.sl
# Check status with:                     squeue -u $USER
#
# Everything starting with "#SBATCH" is a directive read by the scheduler.
# Lines starting with a plain "#" are ordinary comments.

#SBATCH --job-name=hello_longleaf
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2g
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/hello_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/hello_%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=<email-address>

# ---- Load R -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Reset the inherited module environment, then load R. To pin a version, run
# "module avail r" on a login node and replace <version> below.
module purge
module add r

# ---- Run the script ---------------------------------------------------------
# SLURM starts the job in the directory you ran sbatch from, so relative
# paths (hello_longleaf.R, results/, logs/) resolve as expected.
Rscript --vanilla hello_longleaf.R








Directive
Request




--job-name=hello_longleaf
The name shown by squeue


--nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1
One task with one CPU on one node


--mem=2g
Reserve 2 GB of memory


--time=00:10:00
Allow up to ten minutes


--output and --error
Where to write the logs; %j becomes the job ID


--mail-type and --mail-user
Email when the job ends or fails



After the directives, the script loads R and runs the R script with Rscript. Slurm starts the job in the directory you ran sbatch from, so the relative paths to the script, logs/, and results/ resolve as expected.


The R script
The script is ordinary R. The only cluster-specific lines print the host name and Slurm job ID at the start, which makes it easy to confirm from the log that the job ran on a compute node.






Notehello_longleaf.R







hello_longleaf.R

###############################################################################
# hello_longleaf.R -- Example 2: a single, self-contained R job
#
# What it does:
#   1. Simulates a small dataset
#   2. Fits a linear model and computes a few summary numbers
#   3. Saves everything to results/hello_results.rds
#
# Run locally:   Rscript hello_longleaf.R
# Run on Longleaf: sbatch submit_single.sl   (see README.md)
###############################################################################

# ---- 0. Settings you may want to change -------------------------------------
n       <- 500                      # sample size
seed    <- 2026                     # for reproducibility
out_dir <- "results"                # relative to the folder you sbatch from
outfile <- file.path(out_dir, "hello_results.rds")

dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# ---- 1. Report where/when we are running (handy for debugging on the cluster)
cat("Started:   ", format(Sys.time()), "\n")
cat("Host:      ", Sys.info()[["nodename"]], "\n")
cat("Working dir:", getwd(), "\n")
cat("SLURM job: ", Sys.getenv("SLURM_JOB_ID", unset = "(not running under SLURM)"), "\n")

# ---- 2. Simulate data and fit a model ---------------------------------------
set.seed(seed)
x <- rnorm(n)
y <- 1 + 2 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)

# ---- 3. Bundle the results into a list --------------------------------------
results <- list(
  n            = n,
  seed         = seed,
  coefficients = coef(fit),
  r_squared    = summary(fit)$r.squared,
  mean_y       = mean(y),
  sd_y         = sd(y),
  hostname     = Sys.info()[["nodename"]],
  slurm_job_id = Sys.getenv("SLURM_JOB_ID", unset = NA),
  r_version    = R.version.string,
  finished_at  = Sys.time()
)

# ---- 4. Save to disk --------------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(results, outfile)
cat("Saved results to:", normalizePath(outfile), "\n")
cat("Finished:  ", format(Sys.time()), "\n")






Step by step

Copy the folder to Longleaf and go to it. In FileZilla, drag example2_single_job from your computer into your home directory on Longleaf, as shown in Module 2. Then log in and go to it:
ssh <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu
cd ~/example2_single_job
Edit submit_single.sl. Set --mail-user to your email, or delete the two --mail-* lines. Raise --time or --mem if a real job needs more. Jobs that exceed their limits are killed, so ask for a little more than you expect. FileZilla’s View/Edit, described in Module 2, is the easiest way to make this change.
Submit. Slurm replies with Submitted batch job 12345678. That number is the job ID.
sbatch submit_single.sl
Monitor.
squeue -u "$USER"               # pending (PD) or running (R)?
sacct -j 12345678               # state and exit code after it finishes
cat logs/hello_12345678.out     # what the script printed
Look at the results, on Longleaf or after copying them back to your laptop.
module add r
Rscript -e 'str(readRDS("results/hello_results.rds"))'
To work with the file on your laptop, press F5 in FileZilla so the new files appear, then drag results from the Longleaf pane to your computer.







NoteAbout the logs/ folder



Slurm 23.02 and newer create the folder named in --output if it does not exist. Older versions do not, and the job then fails immediately with no output to explain why. The example folder ships with an empty logs/ so it works on either.

title: R on Longleaf
section: Example 3 · Submitting a batch of jobs with parameters
text:
Example 3 · Submitting a batch of jobs with parameters
Instead of editing the R script and resubmitting it for every setting, write each combination of settings as one row of a plain text file, submit a Slurm job array with one task per row, and let each task pass its row to R as command-line arguments. Twelve rows become twelve independent jobs that run in parallel on whatever nodes are free, each saving its own result file. The files are in examples/example3_conditions_array/.

How the pieces fit together
sbatch submit_array.sl
   │   #SBATCH --array=1-12  → Slurm starts 12 tasks, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = 1..12
   │
   └─▶ sh runcode.sh $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID          (task 7 shown)
          │   sed "7q;d" conditions.txt   →   "7 50 0 2"
          │
          └─▶ Rscript run_condition.R 7 50 0 2
                 │   commandArgs() → c("7", "50", "0", "2")
                 │
                 └─▶ results/result_n50_beta0.0_rep02.rds



File
Purpose




make_conditions.R
Builds conditions.txt from an expand.grid() of settings. Rerun it whenever the grid changes.


conditions.txt
One row per job. Space-separated, no header. Columns: row_id n beta rep.


run_condition.R
The worker. Reads four command-line arguments, simulates, and saves one .rds.


runcode.sh
Picks one line of conditions.txt and calls R with it.


submit_array.sl
The Slurm job array submission script.


collect_results.R
Stacks every .rds into one data frame and lists any rows that are missing.





The conditions file
Each row is one job. make_conditions.R builds the file from every combination of two sample sizes, two slopes, and three replications, with the row number as the first column so each job knows its own ID.


conditions.txt

1 50 0 1
2 200 0 1
3 50 0.5 1
4 200 0.5 1
5 50 0 2
6 200 0 2
7 50 0.5 2
8 200 0.5 2
9 50 0 3
10 200 0 3
11 50 0.5 3
12 200 0.5 3







Notemake_conditions.R







make_conditions.R

###############################################################################
# make_conditions.R -- builds conditions.txt for Example 3
#
# Each ROW of conditions.txt is one job in the SLURM array. Columns are
# separated by spaces and there is NO header row (the shell script reads
# lines by number, so a header would be mistaken for condition 1).
#
# Run:  Rscript make_conditions.R
###############################################################################

grid <- expand.grid(
  n    = c(50, 200),           # sample size
  beta = c(0, 0.5),            # true slope
  rep  = 1:3,                  # replication
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Add the row number as the first column so each job knows its own ID.
grid <- cbind(row_id = seq_len(nrow(grid)), grid)

write.table(grid, "conditions.txt",
            row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

cat(sprintf("Wrote conditions.txt with %d rows (use --array=1-%d)\n",
            nrow(grid), nrow(grid)))
print(grid)






The submission script


submit_array.sl

#!/bin/bash
# submit_array.sl -- SLURM job array for Example 3
#
# Submit from inside this folder with:   sbatch submit_array.sl
#
# --array=1-12 launches 12 copies of this script. Each copy gets a different
# value of $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (1, 2, ..., 12), which we use to pick a line
# from conditions.txt. The range MUST match the number of lines in that file
# (wc -l conditions.txt). Add %N to throttle, e.g. --array=1-500%50 runs at
# most 50 at a time.

#SBATCH --job-name=cond_array
#SBATCH --array=1-12
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1g
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/cond_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/cond_%A_%a.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=<email-address>

# %A = the array's master job ID, %a = this task's index, so each task
# gets its own log file, e.g. logs/cond_12345678_7.out

sh runcode.sh $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

The one new directive is --array=1-12. It launches twelve copies of the script, each with a different value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. The range must match the number of lines in conditions.txt. In the log file names, %A is the array’s job ID and %a is the task index, so each task gets its own log.


The glue script
Each task runs this short shell script, which pulls its own line out of conditions.txt and hands the values to R:


runcode.sh

#!/bin/bash
# runcode.sh -- glue between SLURM and R for Example 3
#
# Usage:  sh runcode.sh <line_number>
#
# Picks line <line_number> out of conditions.txt and passes its contents to
# run_condition.R as command-line arguments. submit_array.sl calls this with
# $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, so array task 7 runs row 7 of conditions.txt.

CONDITIONS=conditions.txt

# sed "Nq;d" prints line N of the file and nothing else.
input=$(sed "${1}q;d" $CONDITIONS)

if [ -z "$input" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: no line $1 in $CONDITIONS" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Task $1 -> conditions: $input"

module purge
module add r
Rscript --vanilla run_condition.R $input



The worker script
Only the top of run_condition.R is specific to the array. R receives the arguments as text, so the script converts each one:


run_condition.R (excerpt)

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
if (length(args) != 4) {
  stop("Usage: Rscript run_condition.R <row_id> <n> <beta> <rep>\n",
       "Got ", length(args), " argument(s): ", paste(args, collapse = " "))
}

row_id <- as.integer(args[1])
n      <- as.integer(args[2])
beta   <- as.numeric(args[3])
rep_i  <- as.integer(args[4])

The rest simulates data, fits a model, and saves a result file whose name encodes the condition. The seed is derived from the condition values rather than the task ID, so rerunning row 7 always gives the same answer, and appending rows to conditions.txt never changes earlier results.






Noterun_condition.R







run_condition.R

###############################################################################
# run_condition.R -- Example 3 worker script: ONE row of conditions.txt
#
# Called by runcode.sh as:
#   Rscript --vanilla run_condition.R <row_id> <n> <beta> <rep>
#
# The four values after the script name are one line of conditions.txt.
# R receives them as a character vector from commandArgs(); convert types
# yourself.
###############################################################################

# ---- 1. Read the command-line arguments -------------------------------------
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
if (length(args) != 4) {
  stop("Usage: Rscript run_condition.R <row_id> <n> <beta> <rep>\n",
       "Got ", length(args), " argument(s): ", paste(args, collapse = " "))
}

row_id <- as.integer(args[1])
n      <- as.integer(args[2])
beta   <- as.numeric(args[3])
rep_i  <- as.integer(args[4])

cat(sprintf("=== Row %d: n=%d, beta=%.2f, rep=%d ===\n", row_id, n, beta, rep_i))
cat("Host:", Sys.info()[["nodename"]],
    " SLURM task:", Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID", unset = "(none)"), "\n")

# ---- 2. Seed from the condition, not from the row order ---------------------
# This way re-running row 7 always gives the same answer, and adding rows to
# the bottom of conditions.txt never changes earlier results.
set.seed(1000 * n + 100 * round(beta * 10) + rep_i)

# ---- 3. Do the (trivial) work -----------------------------------------------
x   <- rnorm(n)
y   <- beta * x + rnorm(n)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)

results <- list(
  row_id     = row_id,
  n          = n,
  beta_true  = beta,
  rep        = rep_i,
  beta_hat   = unname(coef(fit)["x"]),
  p_value    = summary(fit)$coefficients["x", "Pr(>|t|)"],
  hostname   = Sys.info()[["nodename"]],
  finished   = Sys.time()
)

# ---- 4. Save with a filename that encodes the condition ---------------------
out_dir <- "results"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
outfile <- file.path(out_dir,
                     sprintf("result_n%d_beta%.1f_rep%02d.rds", n, beta, rep_i))
saveRDS(results, outfile)
cat("Saved:", outfile, "\n")










Notecollect_results.R







collect_results.R

###############################################################################
# collect_results.R -- stack every results/*.rds into one data frame
#
# Run after the array finishes:  Rscript collect_results.R
# Also reports any conditions.txt rows that have no result file (failed or
# still-running tasks), so you know exactly which array indices to resubmit.
###############################################################################

files <- list.files("results", pattern = "\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Found %d result files\n", length(files)))

rows <- lapply(files, function(f) {
  r <- readRDS(f)
  data.frame(row_id = r$row_id, n = r$n, beta_true = r$beta_true, rep = r$rep,
             beta_hat = r$beta_hat, p_value = r$p_value,
             hostname = r$hostname)
})
all_results <- do.call(rbind, rows)
all_results <- all_results[order(all_results$row_id), ]
rownames(all_results) <- NULL
print(all_results)

# Which rows of conditions.txt are missing?
cond <- read.table("conditions.txt",
                   col.names = c("row_id", "n", "beta", "rep"))
missing <- setdiff(cond$row_id, all_results$row_id)
if (length(missing) == 0) {
  cat("\nAll conditions complete.\n")
} else {
  cat("\nMISSING rows (resubmit with --array=",
      paste(missing, collapse = ","), "):\n", sep = "")
  print(cond[cond$row_id %in% missing, ])
}

saveRDS(all_results, "all_results.rds")
cat("Saved all_results.rds\n")






Step by step

Build the conditions file on your laptop or on Longleaf, and note the number of rows.
Rscript make_conditions.R
wc -l conditions.txt
Copy the folder to Longleaf and go to it. Drag example3_conditions_array into your home directory with FileZilla, then log in and go to it:
ssh <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu
cd ~/example3_conditions_array
Edit submit_array.sl. Make --array=1-12 match the row count. This is the line people forget: too small and some conditions never run, too large and the extra tasks fail with “no line N”. Set or delete the --mail-* lines, and remember that --time and --mem apply per task, not to the whole array. For big arrays add a throttle, such as --array=1-2000%100, so you do not monopolize the partition.
Test one row before submitting hundreds. Load R as in Example 1 and run row 1 by hand. If this works, the array will work.
module add r
sh runcode.sh 1
ls results/
Submit and monitor. squeue shows one line per running or pending task.
sbatch submit_array.sl
squeue -u "$USER"
sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
tail logs/cond_<jobid>_7.out
Collect. This prints a table of all results, writes all_results.rds, and lists any rows that have no result file.
Rscript collect_results.R
To rerun only the missing rows, submit again with an explicit list. A command-line --array overrides the one inside the file.
sbatch --array=3,8,11 submit_array.sl



Adapting the pattern to your own project

Changing which variables are passed. Three places must agree: the columns of the grid in make_conditions.R, the number and order of arguments read in run_condition.R, and the column names used to read conditions.txt back in collect_results.R. The glue script and the submission script do not care how many columns there are.
Strings are fine as values, such as high or identity, as long as they contain no spaces. R receives everything as character; convert with as.integer() or as.numeric() as needed.
Paths. As in Example 2, everything is relative to the folder you run sbatch from. Anything large belongs in your personal data space, /hickory/users/<o>/<n>/<onyen> (Module 2), rather than your home directory.
Several methods on the same conditions. Either add a method column to the grid, or keep one conditions.txt and write one submission script per method that passes the method name as an extra argument.

title: Getting Started with Longleaf
text:
This workshop follows the path from first login to a submitted R job. The four modules can be presented live and remain available afterward as a practical reference.
Audience: Researchers who are new to Longleaf or shared computing clusters
Format: Four short modules with demonstrations and reusable examples

Introduction to Longleaf

Open module

Open module

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
A Longleaf account is separate from your ONYEN and is not created automatically. Complete the following steps to obtain an account:

Open UNC Research Computing’s Request a Cluster Account page.
Choose Longleaf Cluster as the subscription type and submit the form.
Wait for the email saying the account has been created. Until it arrives, logins to Longleaf and Open OnDemand fail.

Once the account exists, your username on Longleaf is your ONYEN and the password is your ONYEN password.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Connecting to the cluster
Longleaf is reachable directly from the campus network. From anywhere else, connect to the UNC VPN first. Everything you do with Longleaf needs this connection.
UNC ITS distributes and supports the campus VPN client. Open UNC’s Secure Access On- and Off-Campus page and follow its VPN Access link for the current installation instructions. To connect, use vpn.unc.edu. Authenticate with your Carolina Sign-In Key, or use your ONYEN password and complete Duo verification when prompted.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Ways to connect








Method
Best for
What the user sees




Terminal (ssh)
Direct command-line work; what Modules 3 and 4 use
A shell prompt on a login node


Open OnDemand
RStudio in the browser, a terminal without installing one, browsing files
A dashboard with Files, Shell, and Interactive Apps


FileZilla
Moving files between your computer and Longleaf
A two-pane file browser: your computer on the left, Longleaf on the right




Which should you use?
All three, for different things. The terminal is where Modules 3 and 4 happen, because submitting jobs is a command-line task. FileZilla is for moving files in and out. Open OnDemand is for RStudio on a compute node, and it doubles as a terminal on a computer with no ssh client.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Logging in from a terminal
The terminal is the route the rest of this workshop uses. Modules 3 and 4 run every command from a terminal connected to a login node.
On a Mac, open Terminal (in Applications › Utilities) and type:
ssh <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu
On Windows, UNC Research Computing recommends MobaXterm (Home Edition): start a new SSH session with longleaf.unc.edu as the remote host, port 22, and your ONYEN as the username. Windows Terminal and PowerShell also have ssh built in, so the command above works there too.
The first time you connect, ssh asks whether to trust the host; type yes. Then enter your ONYEN password. Nothing appears while you type it, which is normal.
Once connected, the prompt changes to show your ONYEN and the name of a login node. A login node is the place to edit files, load software, and submit jobs. It is shared with everyone else who is logged in, so do not run analyses on it; Module 3 shows how to send them to a compute node.
To leave, type exit. If a program needs to open a graphics window, connect with ssh -X <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu instead.



A successful SSH login to Longleaf from a terminal.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Working through the browser
Open OnDemand is Longleaf’s web portal at https://ondemand.rc.unc.edu. Sign in with your ONYEN and password. It needs a Longleaf account; without one, the page shows instructions for requesting it. If it does not load from off campus, connect to the VPN first.
The dashboard’s menus cover most of what a new user needs:







Menu
What it offers




Files
A file browser for your home directory and other Longleaf storage, with upload and download by drag and drop.


Clusters › Shell Access
A terminal in a browser tab, identical to an ssh session. Useful on a computer without a terminal program.


Interactive Apps › RStudio Server
RStudio running on a compute node. You choose the hours, CPUs, memory, and R module; UNC recommends at least two CPUs. Module 4 uses this.


Jobs › Job Composer
A form-based way to submit batch jobs. This workshop submits jobs from a terminal instead, so the scripts and paths stay the same everywhere.



Sessions started from Interactive Apps wait in the queue like any other job, so start one a few minutes before you need it.



The Open OnDemand dashboard provides browser-based access to files, cluster tools, and interactive applications such as RStudio Server.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Moving files with FileZilla
FileZilla is a free file-transfer program for Mac, Windows, and Linux. It shows your computer on the left and Longleaf on the right, and you move files by dragging them across. It uses the same login as the terminal, so there is nothing to set up on Longleaf.

Install
Download FileZilla Client from https://filezilla-project.org/. The site also offers FileZilla Server, which you do not want. On Windows, the installer may offer additional software during setup; decline it.


Connect
The quickest route is the Quickconnect bar at the top of the window:



Field
Value




Host
sftp://longleaf.unc.edu


Username
your ONYEN


Password
your ONYEN password


Port
22



Click Quickconnect. The first time, FileZilla asks whether to trust the server’s host key; click OK. If the connection times out, confirm that you are on campus or connected to the VPN.
To avoid retyping, save the connection. Open File › Site Manager, click New site, set Protocol to SFTP - SSH File Transfer Protocol, enter the host, port, and your ONYEN as the user, set Logon Type to Ask for password, and click Connect.


Transfer
After connecting, the right pane shows your home directory on Longleaf.

Upload: drag a file or folder from the left pane to the right pane. Dragging a folder copies everything inside it.
Download: drag from the right pane to the left.
Go somewhere else on Longleaf: type a path from the next section into the Remote site box and press Enter.
See new files: FileZilla does not notice files a job wrote after you connected. Press F5 to refresh.

Progress appears in the transfer queue at the bottom of the window.



FileZilla displays files on the local computer in the left pane and files on Longleaf in the right pane.








TipEdit a script in place



Right-click a text file in the Longleaf pane and choose View/Edit. FileZilla opens it in an editor on your computer. When you save, it asks whether to upload the changed file; click Yes. This is enough for small changes such as setting the email address in a submission script.


For very large datasets or transfers you repeat often, command-line tools such as rsync are easier to script. FileZilla covers everything in this workshop.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Where files live
Longleaf’s login and compute nodes can access the same shared storage. A script prepared on a login node can therefore read data and write results while it runs on a compute node.
The main storage locations for new users are below. Two of them start with /hickory, the name of Longleaf’s newer storage system. The name is only a label, in the same tree-naming tradition as Longleaf itself. What matters is the contrast: home is small and backed up, hickory is large and not.

Home directory: /nas/longleaf/home/<onyen> is a relatively small (50 GB), backed-up space for scripts, settings, and personal software, including your R packages. It is not intended for data-intensive computing.
Personal data space: /hickory/users/<o>/<n>/<onyen> provides a much larger location (2 TB) for active and inactive personal research data. It is not backed up. <o> and <n> are the first and second letters of your ONYEN, so the ONYEN jdoe has /hickory/users/j/d/jdoe.
Project space: research groups may have shared storage under /hickory/proj or, for School of Medicine groups, /vast/som. A PI requests it from Research Computing. Its location and quota depend on the group, and it is not backed up by default.

Accounts created before summer 2026 may also have older /work or /users directories. UNC stopped creating /work in July 2026 and /users in August 2026, when /hickory/users became the default. This workshop uses /hickory/users for anything too large for the home directory.

title: Accessing Longleaf
text:
Summary

Request a Longleaf account before trying to connect.
From off campus, connect to the UNC VPN first.
Use SSH for terminal work, Open OnDemand for browser-based tools, and FileZilla for transferring files.
Keep scripts and settings in your backed-up home directory; use /hickory/users for larger data that is not backed up.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
UNC’s effort to acquire a digital computer began in 1951, when Kenan Professor of Mathematics and department chair William M. Whyburn wrote to Chancellor R.B. House. Whyburn had become interested in digital computing through conversations with mathematicians at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, where he worked as a consultant.
UNC began canvassing the campus for interest in 1952. By 1955, eight academic departments had expressed interest: Economics, Business Administration, Mathematics, Mathematical Statistics, Biostatistics, Psychology, Psychometrics, and Physics.
In 1959, UNC-Chapel Hill installed a Sperry Rand UNIVAC 1105 in the basement of Phillips Hall. It was one of the most advanced computers in existence at the time and represented a major institutional investment in scientific and administrative computing.



The UNIVAC 1105 at UNC-Chapel Hill.


The machine was so large and heavy that the floors of Phillips Hall had to be reinforced with steel beams before it could be installed.
The UNIVAC arrived with an important assignment: it was one of only four computers in the United States used to process data for the 1960 U.S. Census. UNC also envisioned uses beyond the census. The University’s new Computation Center was intended to support quantitative work across academic disciplines and help researchers “enlarge the boundaries of human knowledge.”

The UNIVAC arrived with an important assignment: it was one of only four computers in the United States used to process data for the 1960 U.S. Census. UNC also envisioned uses beyond the census. The University’s new Computation Center was intended to support quantitative work across academic disciplines and help researchers “enlarge the boundaries of human knowledge.”

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
The UNIVAC by the numbers

Cost: $2.4 million in 1959—approximately $24 million in 2022 dollars
Weight: 19 tons
Working memory: 36–54 kilobytes
Storage: 5 megabytes of magnetic-tape storage
Capacity: One single-threaded, non-interruptible job at a time

Although those specifications appear extremely limited today, the UNIVAC 1105 was a powerful and advanced machine by the standards of 1959.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
How people accessed it
The UNIVAC was a monolithic computer: one large, centralized machine rather than a collection of independently accessible computers.
Users could not log in, open programs, or interact with the machine directly. Only system administrators operated the computer, so users accessed its computing capabilities through those administrators.
The computer could process only one job at a time. Once a job began, it ran without interruption until it finished or failed. After the 1960 Census work was completed, the machine was used primarily by university departments and administrative units, including UNC Finance and UNC Human Resources.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
section: Compared with a personal computer today
text:
Compared with a personal computer today
For perspective, consider a current lightweight laptop with 16 gigabytes of memory, 512 gigabytes of storage, and a weight of approximately 2.7 pounds.



Feature
UNIVAC 1105
Example current laptop




Working memory
36–54 KB
16 GB


Storage
5 MB of tape
512 GB SSD


Weight
19 tons
2.7 pounds


Access
Through system administrators
Directly by its owner


Workload
One job at a time
Many programs and processes



A laptop with 16 GB of memory has approximately 300,000 times as much working memory as the upper end of the UNIVAC’s reported memory.
A 512 GB solid-state drive holds approximately 100,000 times as much data as the UNIVAC’s 5 MB of tape storage. A single compressed photograph from a modern phone can occupy several megabytes—potentially most of the UNIVAC’s reported storage capacity.
At 19 tons, the UNIVAC was approximately 14,000 times heavier than a 2.7-pound laptop.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
From one job to thousands
The UNIVAC ran one job at a time, and researchers handed their work to operators who ran it when the machine was free. Longleaf’s arrangement is recognizably the same: you hand your work to a scheduler, which runs it when the resources are free. The differences are scale and automation. Longleaf runs many jobs at once across a large pool of computers, the operators have been replaced by software called Slurm, and you talk to it yourself from a terminal. By Module 4, you will submit twelve jobs with one command and collect their results with another.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
Sources

“7 decades of difference: Carolina’s 1st computer and its current cluster,” UNC-Chapel Hill
“Visions of Tomorrow with Computers of Today: UNC’s First Computer in 1959,” UNC University Libraries

title: How Longleaf Works
text: Longleaf is made up of many connected computers that are shared by researchers across UNC. Users prepare their work in one place, then ask the cluster to run it using the resources it needs.

title: How Longleaf Works
section: From your computer to a compute node
text:
From your computer to a compute node


1 · Connect
Connect to Longleaf from a terminal or web browser. You arrive on a login node.


2 · Prepare
Use the login node to organize files, edit code, load software, and describe the resources the work needs.


3 · Schedule
Submit the work as a job. Slurm holds the job in a queue until suitable resources are available.


4 · Compute
A compute node runs the job and writes its output to storage.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
Login nodes and compute nodes
A node is one computer within the cluster. Longleaf nodes serve different purposes:

A login node is the shared entry point. Use it to work with files, edit scripts, run basic commands, and submit jobs.
A compute node supplies the processors and memory that run an analysis.

Users normally do not select or log in directly to a compute node. They request resources through Slurm, which places the work on an appropriate node.






WarningKeep demanding work off the login node



Many people share each login node. Running an analysis there can slow the system for everyone. Submit computational work through Slurm so that it runs on a compute node.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
What is Slurm?
A job is a request to run a program using specified cluster resources. Longleaf uses Slurm, a workload manager and job scheduler, to coordinate those requests.
Users do not normally select a compute node and start an analysis directly. Instead, they tell Slurm what program to run and what resources it needs. Slurm then manages the job from submission through completion.

title: How Longleaf Works
How Longleaf Works
text:
What happens after submission?

Slurm checks the job request and assigns it a unique job ID.
The job enters the queue, usually with a pending status.
Slurm waits until suitable CPUs, memory, and any specialized hardware are available.
Slurm allocates those resources and starts the job on a compute node.
The job finishes or stops, Slurm records its status, and the resources become available again.

A pending job has not necessarily encountered a problem. It may be waiting because the requested resources are currently in use, no available node has enough memory, the job needs specialized hardware, or other jobs currently have higher priority.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
What Slurm does not do
Slurm manages resources and jobs, but it does not rewrite or optimize the program being submitted. In particular:

requesting more CPUs does not make single-threaded code use them;
requesting more memory does not make code run faster; and
Slurm does not automatically know how much time or memory a program will need.

Users therefore need to make reasonable initial requests and refine them using information from completed jobs. Module 3 shows how to submit and monitor jobs and review their resource use.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
What does a job request?
For most jobs, the essential requests are:







Resource
What it means




CPUs
The processor capacity available to the job


Memory
The short-term working space, or RAM, available while the program runs


Time
The maximum amount of time the job is allowed to run


Partition
Which group of nodes the job may use. Most jobs leave this unset; interactive sessions use interact



Asking for more resources does not automatically make a program run faster. A program must be written to use multiple CPUs, and unused memory does not improve its speed. Requests that are close to what the job actually needs also make it easier for Slurm to find a place for the job to run.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
Memory and storage
Memory and storage serve different purposes:

Memory holds the data and instructions a program is actively using. It is temporary and belongs to the compute node running the job.
Storage holds scripts, datasets, logs, and results as files. Files remain available after a job ends.

One useful comparison is a desk and a filing cabinet. Memory is the desk where current work is spread out. Storage is the filing cabinet where materials are kept between tasks. A larger desk lets you work with more material at once, but it does not necessarily make the work faster.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
Key terms







Term
Meaning




Login node
The shared entry computer used to prepare and submit work


Compute node
A computer where scheduled work runs


Slurm
The system that queues jobs and assigns resources


Job
A unit of work submitted to Slurm


Partition
A logical group of compute nodes


Software module
A way to make installed software available

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
Summary
You use a login node to prepare and submit work. Slurm finds appropriate resources, a compute node runs the job, and the results are written to storage.
Later modules show how to connect to Longleaf, submit a job, and choose appropriate resource requests.

title: How Longleaf Works
text:
Sources

“Getting Started on Longleaf,” UNC Research Computing
“SLURM Guide,” UNC Research Computing
“Quick Start User Guide,” SchedMD

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
Describe
Write the commands and resource request.


Submit
Send the job script to Slurm.


Monitor
Check whether the job is pending or running.


Review
Inspect its output, status, and resource use.

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
Describe
Write the commands and resource request.


Submit
Send the job script to Slurm.


Monitor
Check whether the job is pending or running.


Review
Inspect its output, status, and resource use.

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
A first job script
A Slurm job is described in a shell script. Lines beginning with #SBATCH tell Slurm what the job needs; the remaining lines are the commands that run on a compute node.
The downloadable first_job.sl example does not require specialized software:


first_job.sl

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=first_job
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=100m
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --output=first_job_%j.out

echo "Running on $(hostname) as job $SLURM_JOB_ID"
sleep 90
echo "Done"








Directive
Request




--job-name
The name shown in the queue


--ntasks=1
Run one copy of the program


--cpus-per-task=1
Give that task one CPU


--mem=100m
Reserve 100 MB of memory


--time=00:05:00
Allow up to five minutes


--output=first_job_%j.out
Write output to a file where %j becomes the job ID



The job begins in the directory from which you run sbatch. Relative paths in the script are resolved from that directory. Because this script specifies only --output, normal output and error messages are written to the same file.

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
Submit and monitor
Use these commands in the order that you need them:
sbatch first_job.sl
squeue -u "$USER"
scancel <job-id>
sacct -j <job-id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
seff <job-id>



Command
Purpose




sbatch
Submit a job script; Slurm replies with its job ID


squeue
Show your pending and running jobs


scancel
Cancel a job that no longer needs to run


sacct
Show a completed job’s state, exit code, and elapsed time


seff
Summarize the CPU and memory efficiency of a completed job



squeue uses short codes for active jobs:








Code
State
Meaning




PD
Pending
Waiting in the queue; the reason column explains why


R
Running
Running on a compute node


CG
Completing
Finishing its final cleanup before leaving the queue



When a job disappears from squeue, use sacct to see whether it was COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, or OUT_OF_MEMORY.

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
Run the example
From the directory containing first_job.sl:
sbatch first_job.sl           # Slurm prints the new job ID
squeue -u "$USER"             # watch for PD or R
cat first_job_12345678.out    # use the job ID that Slurm printed
The output identifies a compute node rather than a login node. Slurm moved the work to an appropriate machine and recorded the result in a file.

title: Running a Slurm job
text:
Troubleshooting
Begin with the job state, output file, and exit code rather than assuming a single cause.







What you see
What to check




The job remains pending
Read the reason shown by squeue; the requested resources may not currently be available


The job fails immediately
Read its output and inspect State and ExitCode with sacct


command not found
Check the command spelling, software-module commands, and paths


TIMEOUT
Request more time or make the program more efficient


OUT_OF_MEMORY
Review memory use with seff, then adjust the request


Expected output is missing
Check the job state, submission directory, output filename, and error messages

title: R on Longleaf
section: Setting up a project on Longleaf
text:
Setting up a project on Longleaf
Give every project one folder, and lay it out the same way every time:
myproject/
├── analysis.R        # the R script a job runs
├── submit.sl         # the Slurm script that runs it
├── logs/             # what Slurm and R print while the job runs
└── results/          # what the R script saves on purpose
Scripts sit at the top level. logs/ catches the .out and .err files, and results/ holds the files your code writes. Keeping the two apart means a failed run never buries a good result, and ls results/ shows only things worth keeping. A project that reads input files gets a data/ folder beside them.
Three habits make the layout work:

Submit from inside the folder. Slurm starts a job in the directory you ran sbatch from, so cd myproject first. Every relative path in the submission script and in the R code then means the same thing it meant on your laptop.
Use relative paths in your code. saveRDS(fit, "results/fit.rds") works on your laptop and on Longleaf. A hard-coded C:/Users/... or /Users/... path works on neither.
Mirror the folder on your laptop. Build and test the project locally, drag the whole folder to Longleaf with FileZilla, and drag results/ back when the jobs finish. Nothing needs renaming in either direction.

Put the folder in your home directory, /nas/longleaf/home/<onyen>. It is backed up and holds 50 GB, which is plenty for scripts, logs, and modest results. Input data larger than a few gigabytes belongs in your personal data space, /hickory/users/<o>/<n>/<onyen> from Module 2, and the script reads it by its full path:
dat <- readRDS("/hickory/users/j/d/jdoe/survey/wave3.rds")
To create the folder on Longleaf from the terminal:
mkdir -p ~/myproject/logs ~/myproject/results
cd ~/myproject
Or make it on your laptop and upload it with FileZilla. The example2_single_job and example3_conditions_array folders in examples.zip are two projects laid out this way, so copying one and renaming it is the quickest start.
